b: Back in the 16th century, an Italian named Giovanni Della Casa wrote an etiquette manual called Galateo. You’d think a 500-year-old book on manners wouldn’t have much to say to a modern man, and some of it certainly doesn’t apply. (He admonishes people for wearing toothpicks around their necks, which I guess was a thing in 16th-century Italy.) But I was surprised by how much of Della Casa’s advice still holds up today.
Below are 15 evergreen lessons from Galateo on how to be a suave gentleman and not an annoying chooch.
1. Nobody Wants to Hear About Your Dreams
Those who painstakingly recount their dreams with great enthusiasm, making such fuss and marveling so very much that one is left completely worn out just hearing them, are doing something bad.
Thus, one should not annoy others with such stuff as dreams, especially since most dreams are by and large idiotic.

Della Casa complains about people who describe their dreams in painstaking detail. I’m with him on this. Dreams are mostly random nonsense. No one wants to hear about the dream you had last night where you were back in high school, and for some reason your algebra teacher was riding a unicorn and singing “Mambo No. 5” by Lou Bega. It’s interesting to you, but not to anyone else.
2. Don’t Talk About Your Kids All the Time

Nothing comes from the mouths of some others except stories about their children, their wives, or their nannies, and these types are equally to blame. ‘Last night my kid really made me laugh!’ ‘You will never see a cuter baby than my little Momo.’
No one has so little to do that he has the time to respond or even pay attention to such rubbish, and so it exasperates everyone.

Della Casa describes an annoying guy who won’t shut up about how his little boy made him laugh yesterday. That guy is still with us in the 21st century, but now he’s showing you funny videos on his phone of his toddler swearing like a sailor while he laughs hysterically and asks, “Isn’t this hilarious and cute?” No, Bob. It’s not.

Look, I love my kids. They’re a huge part of my life. I’m emotionally invested in them because they’re my progeny. I think they’re so funny and smart and great. But other people aren’t as emotionally invested in my kids, and consequently, they don’t find them so fascinating. Talk about your kids a little bit. But don’t make them the centerpiece of every conversation.
3. Don’t Hijack or Interrupt Other People’s Stories

Others are so avid to speak that they do not let others get a word in edgewise. Just as we sometimes see in a farmer’s coop a chicken snatching grain from another’s beak, so these men take the ideas out of the mouth of the man who began them, and then they start talking.
Therefore, if someone is ready to tell a story, it is not suitable to ruin it for him, nor say you have already heard it.

You’ve probably had this happen. You’re telling a story, and someone jumps in and starts telling it for you and stealing your thunder. In the words of Stephanie Tanner, “How rude!” Let the person finish, and you can add your two cents after. If you’ve already heard the story, Della Casa says you shouldn’t interrupt to say so, either. But what if someone has already told this story a hundred times before? We’ve got some advice on how to handle that situation.

Furthermore, one should be careful not to say things that left out would make the story no less enjoyable, and perhaps even more so. ‘So-and-so, who was the son of the man who lived in Via del Cocomero, you know him, don’t you? His wife was one of the Gianfigliazzi girls. A kind of skinny girl who used to go to Mass at San Lorenzo. What do you mean you don’t know her? Of course, you knew him. A tall old man, with long hair down on his shoulders, don’t you remember him?’ If it did not matter whether the event happened to this man or to another, all this long disquisition would be to no purpose, indeed very tedious to the listeners, who are desirous and impatient to hear the end of the story you began.

Della Casa is talking about people who stuff their stories with details that don’t matter. Does it matter to the story what street the guy’s father lived on? Or whose daughter he married? No, it does not.
I’ll admit I’m guilty of this. I have a tendency to add a bunch of needless details to a story. I’m working on it, though!
When you’re telling a story, get to the point. Brevity is the soul of wit. Long babble just bores and wearies people.

And those who contradict every word and always question and dispute show how little they know of the nature of men, that everyone loves victory and hates being defeated in discussion as well as in action: it goes without saying that contradicting others is the work of enmity, not of friendship. For this reason whoever loves being friendly and sweet in conversation must not have a ready ‘It’s not like that’ or ‘Say what you like, but I am right about this,’ nor place bets on every trifle. Instead, he must make an effort to be conciliatory to others in those matters that are of little account. Victory in such cases turns to our detriment, for in winning a point in a frivolous debate he will often lose some cherished friend; he becomes so maddening to others that they dare not try to stay on friendly terms, so as to escape constant squabbling. And they nickname such ones ‘Mister Know-it-all,’ or ‘Sir Counterpoint,’ or ‘Sir Expert,’ and in old times ‘the Subtle Doctor.’

No one likes a pedantic know-it-all. If you hear someone say something that’s a little off and it’s not a big deal, don’t point it out. If they mispronounce a word or get a date wrong, let it slide. If you don’t agree with some point, you don’t always have to bring up your contrary take.

Della Casa says everybody hates being beaten in an argument as much as they hate losing at anything else, so contradicting someone hurts their pride and engenders resentment. So knock it off, Sir Counterpoint.
6. Stop Giving People Advice They Didn’t Ask For

To offer your advice without having been asked is nothing else but a way of saying that you are wiser than those you are giving advice, and even a reproof for their ignorance and lack of knowledge. For this reason, this should not be done with everyone you know, but only with your best and closest friends and with people who depend on your guidance, or with a stranger who happens to be in great and imminent danger.
Ever had a guy interrupt you while you were at the gym to give you advice on your technique? Annoying!

Della Casa explains that the reason unsolicited advice is so stinkin’ grating is that you’re basically telling the other person you’re smarter than he is. You’re elevating your status, while making the other person feel less than.

Della Casa makes a few exceptions to this rule, including a case where someone is in imminent danger. So unless it looks like a fellow gymgoer is about to kill themselves while squatting, keep your form advice to yourself. (Yes, I realize this whole article is advice you didn’t ask for. But you clicked on it, and I’m counting that as asking.)
7. Don’t Act Entitled to Special Treatment

And they hold everyone hostage by being concerned too much with themselves and their own needs, totally oblivious to others. Moreover they want to have it better than everyone else in every way; they want to sleep in the most comfortable bed, in the nicest room, to sit in the most comfortable chair at the head of the table, and they must be served or seated first. They don’t care for anything unless they themselves thought it up, turning up their noses at everything else, and they think that others ought to wait for them before eating, going out for a ride, playing a game, or having fun.

Della Casa is talking about people who put their own needs above everyone else’s. They expect to be catered to in every situation, with everyone else shaping their schedules and choices around their agenda and preferences. The modern version of this person calls dibs on the master bedroom at the Airbnb or sulks when the restaurant is out of oat milk. They evince main character energy and forget that there are other people in the story too.

There are those who are so dainty and hypersensitive that to live and interact with them is nothing more than finding oneself surrounded by delicate crystal, for they fear the slightest upset, and you must treat and regard them with this in mind. They become as hurt as another if mortally wounded, when you’re not timely or solicitous in saying hello, visiting them, or paying your respects or responding to them.

You probably know thin-skinned people like this. It doesn’t matter what you do or say; they’re going to take offense. In Della Casa’s day, they got huffy if you didn’t greet them quickly enough or swing by their chateau often enough. Today it’s the guy who’s hurt because you didn’t text back within the hour or like his Instagram post. Della Casa says dealing with these people is like handling fragile glass because you have to tiptoe through your interactions with them. Toughen your mental hide, let water roll off your back like a duck’s, and let bygones be bygones. That’s what charming, non-annoying people do.
9. Don’t Brag, But Don’t Belittle Yourself Either
Nor should a man boast of his nobility, his titles, his riches, least of all his intelligence. Nor should he praise at length his past deeds and accomplishments, nor those of his family.

Thus, one should neither belittle himself nor unduly exalt himself. Instead, one should subtract a little from one’s merits, rather than add something to them with words, for even what is good, if flaunted, is displeasing.

When you’re with people, don’t spend the whole time talking about how awesome you are. Or how awesome your kids are (see #2). If your accomplishments have to come up, Della Casa recommends keeping it short and modest and not exaggerating. Better yet, let someone else tout them.

He also exhorts people not to overdo self-deprecation. After a while, it starts to look a little put-on and can read like you’re fishing for compliments; no one wants to have to constantly reassure someone. And if you keep telling people you’re an idiot, eventually they’ll take your word for it.
10. Keep Your Roasts Modest and Funny

You must also know that there is some wit that bites and some that does not bite. Of the former it is enough that you abide by Lauretta’s sage advice: that is, witty sayings should bite the hearer as a sheep does rather than as a dog does; if it bit like a dog it would not be wit but abuse.

Besides all this, you must realize that unless a joke, whether biting or toothless, is pleasant and subtle, those who hear it will take no delight; rather, they will be bored by it, or if they laugh, they laugh at the teller and not the wit.

Della Casa says a jest should bite like a sheep, not like a dog. I’ve never been bitten by a sheep, but I’ll take his word that it’s more of a nibble. A little ribbing between friends — done with genuine humor — is fine (healthy, in fact!). It just shouldn’t be done with pointed teeth. If it is, it’s not a joke anymore. It’s just mean.
Neither at a party nor at the table should one tell depressing tales of woe, nor mention nor call to mind wounds, maladies, deaths, and contagious illnesses, or any other suffering.

You’ve probably seen the Debbie Downer sketches from Saturday Night Live. Everyone’s having a good time. Then Debbie chimes in with something grim, and the sad trombone goes “wah-wahhh.” Debbie is not going to find herself atop the guest list for many parties.

When people are looking to have a good time, they don’t want to hear about death and disease or how horrible things are. Know the situation you’re in and adjust your conversation to meet it. When it’s time to party, add confetti to the parade instead of raining on it.
12. Don’t Look at Your Phone While Talking With Others
Those who occasionally pull a letter out of their pocket to read are equally rude.

Smartphones obviously didn’t exist in the 16th century. But Della Casa did have to put up with people who’d pull a letter out of their pocket in the middle of a conversation and start reading it. Rude!

Every time you check a text while someone’s talking to you, you’re telling them that whatever is happening on your phone is more interesting than they are. Unless you’re running a commonwealth, you can keep your phone tucked away whilst talking to your fellow humans.
Here are some more rules of digital etiquette to keep in mind.
13. Don’t Be Overly Fastidious About Manners
It is also not appropriate, especially not for men, to be susceptible and fastidious, for using manners like this with others seems less like companionship than servitude.

It’s a little funny coming from an etiquette manual, but Della Casa says you can be too nitpicky about manners, to the point where it feels like a tedious and pointless constraint. His example is the guy who meets you at a door and insists you go through first, even when it’d make more sense for him to go first. So you both end up in a real-life Alphonse and Gaston routine.

Manners are about making people feel comfortable. Get too fastidious about them, and you make things uncomfortable. So have good manners, but be cool about it. Otherwise, it becomes unmannerly to be too mannerly.

And just as these and similar actions annoy the senses they pertain to, so grinding one’s teeth, or whistling, screeching, the rubbing of stones and grating of metal are unpleasant to the ear, and so one ought to abstain from such as much as you can. And not only this, but you must watch your singing, especially solo, if you are tone-deaf and sing off key. Few can resist doing this; in fact, it seems the less one’s natural musical talent, the more one sings. There are some who, coughing or sneezing, make such a loud noise that others go deaf; in similar acts they are so indiscreet that those nearby get spritzed in the face. You will also find those who, yawning, bellow and bray like a donkey; or a person with his big mouth wide open who wants you to follow his point, sending out of his mouth that voice—or rather that racket—a deaf-mute makes when he attempts to tell a story.

One must not adopt the habits of some people, such as humming a tune, or imitating the beating of a drum on the table with their fingers, or shuffling their legs, for these actions indicate a real contempt for others.

One of Della Casa’s best diatribes rails against the noises people make. He’s got a beef with teeth grinders, whistlers, people who cough or sneeze so loudly they make you deaf, and people who “bellow and bray like a donkey” when they yawn. He also says not to sing in public if you can’t carry a tune, and he points out that the folks with the worst voices always sing the most. Keep the grating sounds you make to a minimum, so people can enjoy what tranquility there is to be had in an already noisy world.
If you’re a loud sneezer like me (I’ve got the dad sneeze), check out our article on how to tame it.
15. Don’t Show People Gross Stuff and Don’t Ask People to Smell Smelly Stuff

And for the same reason it is not an appropriate behavior, when on the road as sometimes happens one sees something disgusting, to turn to one’s companions and point it out. Even much less should one entreat someone to sniff something that stinks, as some are inclined to do with enormous insistence, even twisting up their noses and saying: ‘Wow, smell this, ugh, it reeks’; rather you should say, ‘Don’t even breathe, it stinks.’

Apparently “Dude, smell this” goes back to at least the 1500s. Della Casa says when you come across something gross, you shouldn’t bring it to everyone’s attention, and you definitely shouldn’t shove something stinky under somebody’s nose and say, “Wow, smell this! It stinks!” Instead, he suggests steering people away from the putrid and gross. Solid advice.
To Be Less Annoying, Don’t Make It All About You

As I read Galateo, I found it oddly comforting to see that so much of human nature doesn’t change and people were just as annoying in 1558 as they are now. Della Casa never had to deal with reply-all emails or guys taking calls on speakerphone at the airport. If he had, I reckon he’d have written a chapter about it.

My big takeaway from this short little book was that a lot of bad manners and being annoying are the result of self-absorption. The guy who tells you his dreams and the guy who’s easily offended are both focused too much on themselves. Good manners, then, simply come down to being mindful of other people. Recognize that they have their own feelings, interests, preferences, and needs, and do what you (reasonably) can do to accommodate them. You’ll not only become more likeable, but you’ll benefit the common good; the more each individual makes life more pleasant for everyone else, the more pleasant life in society becomes as a whole.

The easiest way to become less annoying is to spend a little less time thinking about yourself and a little more time thinking about the people around you. It worked 500 years ago, and it works today.
